notes.objective: Task 1.2: Select and configure FMs.
notes.title: Choose and swap models with Converse
notes.gist: Pick the model on evidence, then call it through one API so you can change providers without rewriting code.
points: Compare models on task quality, latency, price per token, context window and Region availability.
`Converse` and `ConverseStream` use one request shape for every model that supports messages.
Model-only settings go in `additionalModelRequestFields`; tools in `toolConfig`; guardrails in `guardrailConfig`.
Keep the model ID in AppConfig or a parameter, not in code, to switch without redeploying.
`Converse` needs `bedrock:InvokeModel`; `ConverseStream` needs `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`.
notes.tip: Switch providers with no code change points to Converse plus external config such as AppConfig. Trap: writing per-provider InvokeModel payloads or redeploying for each model swap.

notes.objective: Task 1.2: Select and configure FMs.
notes.title: RAG, fine-tuning or distillation?
notes.gist: Use RAG for fresh or private facts, fine-tuning to change behaviour, and distillation to get big-model quality cheaper.
points: RAG needs no training; keep answers current by syncing the knowledge base.
Supervised fine-tuning needs labelled prompt-response pairs; reinforcement fine-tuning uses reward functions in Lambda.
Distillation: a large teacher answers your prompts, then a smaller student is fine-tuned on them.
Training is billed per token times epochs, plus monthly storage for each custom model.
Serve custom models with Provisioned Throughput or an on-demand custom model deployment.
notes.tip: Facts that change weekly mean RAG, not fine-tuning. Cheaper and faster with the same quality on a narrow task means distillation. Trap: retraining just to add new documents.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  Q{What must change?} -->|facts, private data| R[RAG with a knowledge base]
  Q -->|tone, format, task skill| F[Supervised fine-tuning]
  Q -->|cost and latency| D[Distillation: teacher to student]
  Q -->|only instructions| P[Prompt engineering first]
  F --> S[Serve: PT or on-demand deployment]
  D --> S

Format requests to the model spec: JSON bodies, and `messages` with user and assistant roles.

notes.objective: Task 1.4: Design and implement vector store solutions.
notes.title: Knowledge Bases and vector stores
notes.gist: A knowledge base splits your files into chunks, turns them into vectors, stores them, and fetches the closest chunks per question.
points: Managed knowledge base runs ingestion, storage and retrieval; customer-managed lets you pick the vector store.
Stores: OpenSearch Serverless or Managed, Aurora pgvector, Neptune Analytics, S3 Vectors, Pinecone, Redis, MongoDB Atlas.
Index dimensions must match the embedding model, e.g. Titan Text V2: 1,024, 512 or 256.
Binary vectors save storage but lose precision; only OpenSearch stores support them.
Sync is incremental: only added, changed or deleted files are re-ingested via `StartIngestionJob`.
notes.tip: Stale answers after a document change usually mean the data source was not re-synced. Trap: fine-tuning the model or rebuilding the whole index from scratch.

flowchart LR
  S[(S3 and other connectors)] --> P[Parse + chunk]
  P --> E[Embedding model]
  E --> V[(Vector store)]
  Q([Question]) --> E2[Embed the query]
  E2 --> V
  V --> R[Top chunks + citations]
  R --> M{{FM writes the answer}}

notes.objective: Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation.
notes.title: Pick the right chunking strategy
notes.gist: How you cut documents decides what search can find: chunks too big bury the answer, too small lose context.
points: Default: about 300 tokens per chunk, keeping whole sentences.
Fixed-size: you set maximum tokens and an overlap percentage between neighbouring chunks.
Hierarchical: search small child chunks, then return their larger parent for context.
Semantic: splits where meaning shifts; costs extra because it uses a foundation model.
No chunking: one chunk per file; you lose page-number citations and page filtering.
notes.tip: Precise matches but answers lack surrounding context points to hierarchical chunking. Trap: semantic chunking when cost is the priority, or no chunking for long files.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  D[Document] --> C{Content shape?}
  C -->|uniform prose| F[Fixed-size + overlap]
  C -->|long structured manuals| H[Hierarchical parent/child]
  C -->|topics shift often| S[Semantic chunking]
  C -->|already split small| N[No chunking]

notes.objective: Task 1.5: Design retrieval mechanisms for FM augmentation.
notes.title: Make retrieval more relevant
notes.gist: When RAG pulls the wrong chunks, tune the search: mix keyword and vector search, filter, rerank, and split complex questions.
points: Hybrid search mixes semantic and keyword matching; helps with product codes and exact names.
Hybrid needs a store with a filterable text field: RDS, OpenSearch Serverless or MongoDB.
Metadata filters narrow results by attributes such as department, date or document type.
A reranker model rescores retrieved chunks and overrides the default ranking; text only.
Query decomposition breaks a multi-part question into sub-queries before retrieving.
notes.tip: Exact part numbers missed by vector search point to hybrid search; one team's documents only points to metadata filters. Trap: a bigger model instead of fixing retrieval.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q([Complex question]) --> D[Query decomposition]
  D --> H[Hybrid search: vector + keyword]
  F[Metadata filter] -.-> H
  H --> R[Reranker model]
  R --> K[Top-k chunks]
  K --> M{{FM answer}}

notes.objective: Task 1.6: Implement prompt engineering strategies and governance for FM interactions.
notes.title: Prompt Management and Flows
notes.gist: Store prompts as versioned templates with variables, then chain prompts, knowledge bases and code into a visual workflow.
points: A managed prompt holds the message, model and inference settings, plus variables filled at runtime.
Variants let you compare wording or models side by side and keep the best one.
Flows link prompt, knowledge base, Lambda and condition nodes; versions are immutable snapshots.
Apps call `InvokeFlow` on an alias; repoint the alias to roll forward or back.
With a managed prompt in Converse you cannot also send `system`, `inferenceConfig` or `toolConfig`.
notes.tip: Reusable, versioned, reviewed prompts across teams means Prompt Management; chained steps with branching and little code means Flows. Trap: prompts hardcoded inside Lambda functions.

  V --> S[Save version]
  S --> F[Flow: prompt node]
  F --> C{Condition node}
  C -->|needs facts| K[(Knowledge base node)]
  C -->|else| L[Lambda node]

summary.tests: Whether you can pick a model, feed it clean data, build a RAG pipeline that retrieves the right chunks, and manage prompts like code.
must_know: Converse gives one request shape for all message models; keep the model ID in config.
RAG for changing or private facts; fine-tuning for behaviour; distillation for cheaper, faster.
Custom models are served by Provisioned Throughput or an on-demand custom model deployment.
Knowledge base sync is incremental: only added, changed or deleted files are re-ingested.
Default chunking is about 300 tokens; hierarchical returns parent chunks; semantic costs extra.
Hybrid search, metadata filters, rerankers and query decomposition fix poor retrieval.
Prompt Management stores versioned templates with variables; Flows chain nodes and deploy via aliases.
traps: Fine-tuning to add new documents, when syncing a knowledge base is the fix.
Blaming or swapping the model when retrieval returns the wrong chunks.
Hardcoding prompts and model IDs in Lambda instead of managed, versioned config.

cards.q: Which Bedrock API gives one request shape for every model that supports messages, so you can swap providers without rewriting code?
cards.a: `Converse` (and `ConverseStream` for streaming). Keep the model ID in config such as AppConfig, not in code, to switch models without redeploying.

cards.q: Which approach fits changing or private facts, which fits changing model behaviour, and which fits a cheaper, faster model?
cards.a: RAG for changing or private facts; fine-tuning for behaviour; distillation (big teacher, smaller student) for cheaper, faster results with the same quality on a narrow task.

cards.q: How do you serve a custom model in Bedrock?
cards.a: With Provisioned Throughput or an on-demand custom model deployment.

cards.q: What does a knowledge base sync re-ingest, and which API call starts the ingestion?
cards.a: Only added, changed or deleted files, because sync is incremental. The call is `StartIngestionJob`.

cards.q: What is the default chunk size for a knowledge base?
cards.a: About 300 tokens per chunk, keeping whole sentences.

cards.q: Which chunking strategy returns the larger parent chunk, and which one costs extra?
cards.a: Hierarchical searches small child chunks and returns their larger parent; semantic splits where meaning shifts and costs extra because it uses a foundation model.

cards.q: Name four techniques that fix poor retrieval in a RAG pipeline.
cards.a: Hybrid search (semantic plus keyword), metadata filters, a reranker that rescores chunks, and query decomposition of multi-part questions.

cards.q: What does Prompt Management store, and how do Flows reach production?
cards.a: Versioned prompt templates with variables; Flows chain nodes and deploy via aliases that apps call with `InvokeFlow`.

cards.q: Trap: a team wants the model to answer from newly added documents. Is fine-tuning the fix?
cards.a: No. Syncing the knowledge base is the fix; RAG needs no training. Retraining just to add documents is the trap.

cards.q: Trap: RAG answers are wrong and the model looks to blame. What should you check before swapping it?
cards.a: Whether retrieval returned the wrong chunks. Tune retrieval instead of blaming or swapping the model.

cards.q: Trap: prompts and model IDs are hardcoded inside Lambda functions. What should you use instead?
cards.a: Managed, versioned config: Prompt Management for prompts, and AppConfig or a parameter for the model ID.

cards.q: What must a vector index's dimensions match, and what sizes does Titan Text V2 offer?
cards.a: The embedding model's dimensions. Titan Text V2 offers 1,024, 512 or 256.

cards.q: Invoices, call recordings and video must go through one pipeline. Which managed service fits?
cards.a: Bedrock Data Automation: documents, images, audio and video to structured output through one API, not custom OCR and Lambda glue.

cards.q: In a `Converse` request, where do model-only settings, tools and guardrails go?
cards.a: Model-only settings in `additionalModelRequestFields`, tools in `toolConfig`, guardrails in `guardrailConfig`.

cards.q: When you use a managed prompt in `Converse`, which request fields can you not also send?
cards.a: `system`, `inferenceConfig` and `toolConfig`.

notes.objective: Task 2.1: Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations.
notes.title: AgentCore: run agents in production
notes.gist: AgentCore is a set of managed building blocks for hosting, connecting, securing and watching agents built with any framework or model.
points: Runtime: serverless hosting with true session isolation and support for long-running async agents.
Memory: short-term for multi-turn chats, long-term that persists across sessions.
Gateway: turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools; Identity plugs into Cognito, Okta, Entra ID.
Policy checks every tool call against rules; Observability emits OpenTelemetry traces.
Code Interpreter and Browser give agents sandboxed code runs and managed web sessions.
notes.tip: Take a LangGraph or Strands agent to production with isolation and memory means AgentCore Runtime plus Memory. Trap: hand-building ECS hosting and a DynamoDB memory layer.

  R --> G[Gateway: MCP tools]
  G --> L[Lambda, APIs, SaaS]

  P[Policy] -.-> G
  R --> O[Observability: OTEL traces]

notes.objective: Task 2.1: Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations.
notes.title: Strands Agents and MCP tools
notes.gist: Strands is the open-source agent SDK from AWS: give it a model, a prompt and tools, and the model drives the loop.
points: Open source, Python and TypeScript; works with Bedrock and other model providers.
Tools come from your own functions or from any MCP server through an MCP client.
Multi-agent patterns let specialist agents share a larger task.
Deploys to AgentCore, Lambda, Fargate, EKS or EC2, with metrics, traces and logs.
MCP servers: Lambda for light stateless tools, ECS for heavy or long-running tools.
notes.tip: A standard way for agents to reach many tools means MCP. Trap: a custom integration per tool, or putting a heavy, stateful MCP server on Lambda.

notes.objective: Task 2.1: Implement agentic AI solutions and tool integrations.
notes.title: Safe agent workflows with Step Functions
notes.gist: Wrap model and agent steps in a workflow that sets limits, retries, timeouts and human approval before risky actions.
points: Step Functions calls Bedrock `InvokeModel` directly, with no Lambda glue needed.
Cap iterations or set stop conditions so a reasoning loop cannot run forever.
Human review: pause on a callback task token until a person approves.
Circuit breaker: after repeated failures, stop calling the model and serve a fallback.
IAM roles limit which tools and resources each step can reach.
notes.tip: Refunds over a limit need a person to approve means Step Functions with a human approval callback. Trap: trusting the system prompt alone to prevent risky actions.

  C -->|yes| H[Wait for human approval]
  H -->|approved| A
  H -->|rejected| R[Stop and notify]
  M -.->|repeated errors| B[Circuit breaker: fallback]

notes.objective: Task 2.4: Implement FM API integrations.
notes.title: Stream responses in real time
notes.gist: Send tokens to the user as they are generated, so text appears at once and long answers do not time out.
points: `ConverseStream` and `InvokeModelWithResponseStream` return tokens as generated; plain calls wait for all.
Streaming also avoids client read timeouts on long outputs.
Push chunks to browsers over API Gateway WebSockets or server-sent events.
Watch the `TimeToFirstToken` metric for how fast replies feel.
Streaming needs the `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream` permission, separate from `InvokeModel`.
notes.tip: Users wait too long before seeing anything means streaming. Trap: batch inference, caching or a bigger model when the real problem is time to first token.

  U([Browser]) -->|WebSocket| G[API Gateway]

notes.objective: Task 2.4: Implement FM API integrations.
notes.title: Resilient calls: retries, fallbacks, routing
notes.gist: Expect throttling and outages: retry with backoff, fail over to other Regions or models, and send easy prompts to cheap models.
points: `ThrottlingException` is HTTP 429: retry with exponential backoff and jitter, or SDK adaptive mode.
On-demand capacity is shared, so throttles can happen even under your quota.
Cross-Region inference profiles spread load over several Regions in one geography.
Intelligent prompt routing picks between models in one family per request to balance quality and cost.
AWS X-Ray traces calls across services to show which hop is failing.
notes.tip: Intermittent 429s at peak means backoff plus cross-Region inference. Trap: buying Provisioned Throughput for spiky traffic, or retrying instantly in a tight loop.

notes.title: Plug GenAI into enterprise systems
notes.gist: Connect models to existing apps loosely: events and queues for async work, one gateway for control, pipelines for safe releases.
points: EventBridge and SQS decouple producers from slow model calls so work runs asynchronously.
API Gateway fronts models with auth, request validation, throttling and usage plans.
A central GenAI gateway gives every team the same logging, quotas, guardrails and model access.
CodePipeline and CodeBuild run prompt and model tests, security scans and rollbacks.
Data must stay on premises: AWS Outposts. Ultra-low latency at the edge: AWS Wavelength.

summary.tests: Whether you can build agents and tool integrations, call models reliably at scale, and wire GenAI into existing enterprise systems safely.
must_know: Action groups use an OpenAPI schema or function details, run by Lambda or return of control.
Bedrock Agents Classic is closed to new customers; new agent builds point to AgentCore.
AgentCore: Runtime, Memory, Gateway for MCP tools, Identity, Policy, Observability, Evaluations.
Strands is the open-source agent SDK; MCP is the standard way to plug in tools.
Step Functions adds stop conditions, retries, circuit breakers and human approval around model calls.
Stream with ConverseStream for fast first tokens and fewer read timeouts.
429 ThrottlingException: exponential backoff with jitter, then cross-Region inference.
traps: Relying on the prompt alone to stop risky agent actions instead of workflow controls.
Synchronous calls for bulk or slow work that should go through SQS, events or batch.
Provisioned Throughput to fix spiky throttling that backoff and cross-Region inference solve.

cards.q: What defines a Bedrock Agent action group, and what runs it?
cards.a: An OpenAPI schema or function details; it is executed by Lambda or returned to your app (return of control).

cards.q: Bedrock Agents Classic is closed to new customers. Where does AWS point new agent builds?
cards.a: To Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

cards.q: Name the AgentCore building blocks.
cards.a: Runtime, Memory, Gateway (MCP tools), Identity, Policy, Observability and Evaluations.

cards.q: Which open-source SDK from AWS builds agents, and what is the standard way to plug in tools?
cards.a: Strands Agents is the open-source agent SDK; MCP is the standard way to plug in tools.

cards.q: Which service adds stop conditions, retries, circuit breakers and human approval around model and agent calls?
cards.a: AWS Step Functions. It can call Bedrock `InvokeModel` directly, with no Lambda glue needed.

cards.q: Which API gets the first tokens to users fast and avoids read timeouts on long answers?
cards.a: `ConverseStream` (or `InvokeModelWithResponseStream`): it returns tokens as they are generated instead of waiting for the full answer.

cards.q: How do you handle an HTTP 429 `ThrottlingException` from Bedrock?
cards.a: Retry with exponential backoff and jitter (or SDK adaptive mode), then add cross-Region inference.

cards.q: Trap: refunds over a limit need approval. Is a strict system prompt enough to stop risky agent actions?
cards.a: No. Use workflow controls: Step Functions pausing on a callback task token until a person approves, plus IAM roles limiting each step.

cards.q: Trap: thousands of uploads need model processing and nobody is waiting. Why are synchronous API calls wrong?
cards.a: They time out under load. Decouple with an S3 event to SQS to Lambda (EventBridge and SQS), or use batch.

cards.q: Trap: intermittent 429s appear at peak with spiky traffic. Is buying Provisioned Throughput the fix?
cards.a: No. Exponential backoff with jitter plus cross-Region inference solve spiky throttling. Retrying instantly in a tight loop is also a trap.

cards.q: Which alias do you use to test a Bedrock Agent, and what must production call?
cards.a: Test on `TSTALIASID`; production calls an alias that points to a numbered version, not the test alias.

cards.q: You must take a LangGraph or Strands agent to production with session isolation and memory. Which service fits?
cards.a: AgentCore Runtime plus Memory, not hand-built ECS hosting with a DynamoDB memory layer.

cards.q: Where should you host an MCP server for light stateless tools, and where for heavy or long-running tools?
cards.a: Lambda for light stateless tools; ECS for heavy or long-running tools.

cards.q: Which AWS service fits when data must stay on premises, and which fits ultra-low latency at the edge?
cards.a: AWS Outposts for data that must stay on premises; AWS Wavelength for ultra-low latency at the edge.

cards.q: Which IAM permission does `ConverseStream` need, and is it the same as for `Converse`?
cards.a: `bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream`; it is separate from `bedrock:InvokeModel`, which `Converse` uses.

notes.objective: Task 3.1: Implement input and output safety controls.
notes.title: Guardrails: the six safeguards
notes.gist: A guardrail is a reusable safety policy that checks both the user's prompt and the model's answer, for any model.
points: Content filters: hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct and prompt attack, each with a strength.
Denied topics block whole subjects; word filters block exact words such as competitor names.
Sensitive information filters block or mask PII, plus your own regex patterns.
Contextual grounding flags unsupported answers; Automated Reasoning checks answers against logical rules.
Attach by guardrail ID and version on the inference call, or call `ApplyGuardrail` alone.
notes.tip: Same safety rules for a self-hosted or non-Bedrock model means `ApplyGuardrail`; never give investment advice means a denied topic. Trap: word filters to block a whole topic.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P([Prompt]) --> G1[Input check: filters, topics, PII]
  G1 -->|violation| X[Blocked message]
  G1 --> M{{Model}}

cards.q: Name the six Bedrock Guardrails safeguards.
cards.a: Content filters, denied topics, word filters, sensitive information (PII) filters, contextual grounding check and Automated Reasoning checks.

cards.q: Which API applies the same guardrail policy without invoking a model, even for models outside Bedrock?
cards.a: `ApplyGuardrail`, for example for a self-hosted or non-Bedrock model.

cards.q: With `InvokeModel`, what must you do so the prompt attack filter actually checks user input?
cards.a: Wrap the user input in guardrail input tags; untagged input is not filtered for prompt attacks.

cards.q: Does Bedrock share your prompts and outputs with model providers or use them for training?
cards.a: No. Bedrock neither shares prompts or outputs with model providers nor uses them for training.

cards.q: Which VPC endpoint type keeps Bedrock traffic private, and what do endpoint policies do?
cards.a: Interface endpoints (PrivateLink), with no internet gateway or NAT needed; endpoint policies limit which actions and resources can be used through them.

cards.q: Which Bedrock resources can a customer managed KMS key encrypt?
cards.a: Customization jobs and custom models, agents, ingestion jobs and evaluations.

cards.q: Which logs capture the full prompt and response text of Bedrock calls: CloudTrail or invocation logging?
cards.a: Invocation logging only. CloudTrail records who called which API and when, not the prompt or response text.

cards.q: Trap: you must flag RAG answers not supported by the retrieved documents. Do content filters or denied topics help?
cards.a: No. They judge harm, not accuracy. The contextual grounding check scores grounding and relevance and blocks answers under your threshold.

cards.q: Trap: do guardrails scan retrieved chunks or tool results for prompt attacks?
cards.a: No. They check prompts and answers only; tool results and tool definitions are not checked, so validate them yourself.

cards.q: Trap: can a NAT gateway or a gateway endpoint give Bedrock a private network path?
cards.a: No. Bedrock needs an interface VPC endpoint; gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.

cards.q: Which guardrail safeguard blocks a whole subject such as investment advice, and which blocks exact words such as competitor names?
cards.a: Denied topics block whole subjects; word filters block exact words. Using word filters to block a whole topic is the trap.

cards.q: Which service finds PII stored in an S3 data lake before indexing, and which masks card numbers in chatbot replies?
cards.a: Amazon Macie finds PII in S3; a guardrail sensitive information (PII) filter masks it in replies. Mixing up these two jobs is the trap.

cards.q: Name the four Bedrock interface endpoint services.
cards.a: `bedrock`, `bedrock-runtime`, `bedrock-agent` and `bedrock-agent-runtime`.

cards.q: Which tasks does the contextual grounding check support, and which does it not?
cards.a: It supports summarisation, paraphrasing and question answering, but not conversational chatbot QA.

cards.q: Which SageMaker feature documents a model's intended use, limits and evaluation results for governance?
cards.a: SageMaker model cards.

cards.q: What does Bedrock batch inference cost compared with on-demand, and how do jobs get their input and output?
cards.a: About 50% of the on-demand price; asynchronous jobs read JSONL prompts from S3 and write results to S3.

cards.q: What do the Standard, Flex and Priority service tiers each offer?

cards.q: How should you order a prompt for caching, and which inference mode does prompt caching not apply to?

cards.q: Which `AWS/Bedrock` CloudWatch metric counts throttled requests?

notes.title: Troubleshoot common GenAI failures
notes.gist: Most failures are too much context, throttling, wrong retrieval or a vague prompt; logs and traces show which one.
points: Truncated or rejected long inputs: check the context window; chunk, summarise or trim history.
429 `ThrottlingException`: backoff, quota increase, cross-Region inference.
Read timeouts on long answers: stream with `ConverseStream` or raise the client timeout.
Irrelevant answers: inspect retrieved chunks, chunking and embeddings before blaming the prompt.
Format errors: validate output against a schema and compare prompt versions in logs.
notes.tip: Map the symptom to its layer: quota, retrieval, prompt or context window. Trap: moving to a bigger model when logs show retrieval returned the wrong chunks.

flowchart TB
  S([Bad result]) --> Q{Symptom?}
  Q -->|429 errors| T[Backoff, quota, cross-Region]
  Q -->|truncated output| C[Context window, max tokens]
  Q -->|wrong facts| R[Check retrieved chunks]
  Q -->|bad format| F[Schema validation]

source.title: How do I troubleshoot InvokeModel API errors in Amazon Bedrock?

summary.tests: Whether you can measure answer quality, test retrieval and agents separately, release changes safely, and trace a failure to the right layer.
must_know: Bedrock evaluations: programmatic metrics, LLM-as-a-judge, or human reviewers on your dataset.
LLM-as-a-judge needs a separate evaluator model and returns scores with explanations.
You can judge outside models by supplying your own response data.
Retrieve-only RAG jobs score context relevance and context coverage; coverage needs ground truth.
Golden datasets, quality gates and canary releases protect against regressions.
Map symptoms to layers: 429 is quota, truncation is context, wrong facts is retrieval.
traps: BLEU or ROUGE for open-ended quality when an LLM judge or humans fit better.
Changing the model before checking whether retrieval returned the right chunks.
Judging agents only on final text, ignoring tool choices and traces.

cards.q: What three ways do Bedrock evaluations score a model on your own prompt dataset?
cards.a: Programmatic metrics, an LLM-as-a-judge (a second model scores each response), or human reviewers.

cards.q: What does an LLM-as-a-judge job need besides the generator model, and what does it return?
cards.a: A separate evaluator model; it returns a score plus an explanation for each response.

cards.q: How do you evaluate a model that is hosted outside Bedrock?
cards.a: Bring your own inference responses to the evaluation job.

cards.q: Which metrics does a retrieve-only RAG evaluation score, and which one needs ground-truth reference texts?
cards.a: Context relevance and context coverage; context coverage needs ground-truth reference texts in the dataset.

cards.q: Which three practices protect against regressions when you change a prompt, model or data source?
cards.a: A golden dataset of fixed questions with known good answers, automated quality gates that block a release when scores drop, and canary releases.

cards.q: Map each symptom to its layer: HTTP 429, truncated output and wrong facts.
cards.a: 429 is quota (throttling); truncation is the context window; wrong facts is retrieval.

cards.q: Trap: you need to judge open-ended quality such as tone or helpfulness. Are BLEU or ROUGE the right metrics?
cards.a: No. Use an LLM-as-a-judge or human reviewers, which fit open-ended quality better than BLEU or ROUGE.

cards.q: Trap: answers are wrong though the model is strong. What do you run first before swapping the generator model?
cards.a: A retrieve-only evaluation, to check context relevance and whether retrieval returned the right chunks.

cards.q: Trap: you grade an agent only on its final answer text. What else must you measure?
cards.a: Tool choices and their inputs, via traces: task completion rate, tool choice accuracy, number of steps and latency.

cards.q: Which built-in metrics can an LLM-as-a-judge job score, and how do you cover business rules like brand voice?
cards.a: Built-in metrics include correctness, completeness, faithfulness, helpfulness, coherence and harmfulness; add custom metrics for business rules.

cards.q: What format and size limit apply to a Bedrock RAG evaluation dataset?
cards.a: JSON Lines, up to 1,000 prompts per evaluation.

cards.q: Which evaluation type fits brand tone or helpfulness at scale, and which fits regulated content?
cards.a: LLM-as-a-judge for tone or helpfulness at scale and low cost; human evaluation (staff or subject experts) for expert sign-off on regulated content.

cards.q: Judge models have biases. What two habits keep an LLM-as-a-judge evaluation trustworthy?
cards.a: Keep the rubric fixed and spot-check with humans. Letting the same model judge itself is the trap.

cards.q: Which AgentCore features score agents and trace slow or failing steps?
cards.a: Evaluations scores agents before and after deployment; Observability uses OpenTelemetry traces to find slow or failing steps.

cards.q: Model output comes back in the wrong format. What two actions does troubleshooting call for?
cards.a: Validate the output against a schema and compare prompt versions in the logs.
